chapter: New Orleans bands, Oliver and Armstrong
title: Armstrong's Hot Five and Hot Seven: new form or new emphasis
summary: Perhanis argues Armstrong created a new form. Rose says Armstrong was a unique genius, and the Hot Five and Seven kept the ensemble form with more emphasis on solos. A reel change interrupts.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Now, Al, speaking about the Oliver Band and Louis, how, given the fact that jazz can be defined, or you define jazz as a strict ensemble form in 2-4-4-4 time, with hardly any soloing, how do you explain that someone like Louis, who was born here and played here, ends up changing what I would consider to be the form of jazz to a new form? Although you would say that once the original form was gone, there wasn't a new one to replace it. But let me challenge you with the idea that Louis created a new form for jazz, let's say that's exemplified in the Hot 5, Hot 7 recordings.

Well, of course, there's no question that Louis continued in the New Orleans jazz tradition in the Hot 5 and Hot 7s, even though there was a somewhat greater emphasis on the solo work in those things. Louis didn't move away from...
Okay, the second rail's on, Al. Okay. All right. Thanks.

Goodbye. Bye-bye. What I was asking, Al, was that, isn't there a new form of jazz or a new jazz style created in those Hot 5 and Hot 7, which features so predominantly the solo, and not only the solo instrument, but a whole new conception of jazz playing by Louis Armstrong, we'll say.

Well, there are two aspects to what you just raised. One, of course, is the fact that Louis was a unique musical genius who fits into any era, into any style, into any form. And so far as I knew, there was literally nothing that he could not do. So it is very difficult to be able to judge anything that takes place on the basis of Louis' performance, because he was that much of an artist that he virtually transcended everything, anything formal that could have taken place in the 20th century. And it is also true that the Hot 5 and the Hot 7 are stylistically different from authentic New Orleans music in the stylistic tradition of New Orleans music. However, in spite of that, the form in which he played remains the same. The form remained the ensemble form.
You see? And it is just a change in emphasis that was produced in the Hot 5 recordings.
Change of emphasis to the solo.
Yeah. So the form hasn't changed.
The form has not changed in those things.
